title: The Flower of Evil
full_review:
Veteran French film director Claude Chabrol returns to a favorite theme -- the sinister secrets of a bourgeois family -- in the stylish psychological drama "The Flower of Evil" (Palm).

After several years of living in Chicago, twentysomething Francois Charpin-Vasseur (Benoit Magimel) returns to his prosperous family home outside Bordeaux where he warmly embraces elderly Aunt Line (Suzanne Flon). Four generations of Charpins and Vasseurs have been marrying each other: his father Gerard (Bernard Le Coq) married his stepmother Ann (Nathalie Baye) after their spouses were killed in an accident. She has since become politically ambitious and, much to her husband's distaste, Ann is running for mayor.

With one electrifying, mutual glance, Ann's gorgeous, college-student daughter Michele (Melanie Doutey) makes clear she has been pining for cousin Francois' return, and that he will be unable to resist.

The family reunion, peppered with remarks about gauche Americans, is disrupted when Ann's running mate (Thomas Chabrol, the director's son, in an underwritten role) shows them a leaflet being circulated that discredits the family. Among the charges is that Aunt Line's Nazi sympathizer father died under highly suspicious circumstances. This murky past is why Gerard doesn't want his wife, and the family by extension, to have a high profile.

Michele and Francois go away for a romantic weekend together, both admitting they don't care for his father, a longtime, unrepentant philanderer. Aunt Line chimes in along similar lines -- when she's not distracted by disturbing memories from the Nazi occupation. As election day arrives, Gerard has already made a casual new conquest, but now looks closer to home for extramarital excitement.

Also scripted by Chabrol, the film is a beautifully acted, character-driven piece. Gerard's haughty arrogance, Ann's political drive, Michele's seductiveness, the aunt's unraveling and Francois' malaise shine through the carefully nuanced performances Chabrol elicited from his cast. With disciplined finesse, he delicately peels away the facade of this seemingly classy family to reveal a history of incest, betrayal and murder that has gone unacknowledged. However, this familial flower of evil wilts in the final scenes with a wispy ending that is supposed to bring matters full circle but does not convincingly capture the theme of multigenerational guilt transferred and transformed.

Yet for admirers of understated films where psychological subtext trumps more common depictions of sex and violence, this adult tale of illicit relationships and concealed crimes may prove provocative.

Subtitles.

Because of its acceptance of premarital sex, fleeting violence, some crass references and an instance of rough language, the USCCB Office for Film & Broadcasting classification is A-III -- adults. Not rated by the Motion Picture Association of America.
